item.title: Brain Tissue Proportionality and General Cognitive Ability Across Three Adult Cohorts
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract General cognitive ability may relate to the proportional allocation of brain tissue beyond overall tissue volume. We examined five FreeSurfer compartments using compositional data analysis: cortical gray matter, cerebral white matter, subcortical gray matter, total cerebellum, and brainstem. Human Connectome Project Young Adult data (HCP-YA; N = 1,101) provided discovery estimates; the Dallas Lifespan Brain Study (DLBS; N = 418) and Amsterdam Open MRI Collection ID1000 (AOMIC; N = 926) provided independent cohort tests. Four isometric log-ratio coordinates represented composition, with age, sex, and log total analyzed tissue volume included separately. Composition explained additional cognitive variance in DLBS (partial R² = 4.20%, p = .00154) and AOMIC (partial R² = 1.35%, p = .014). The total-cerebellum-to-cerebral-white-matter contrast selected in HCP was positive in both replication cohorts: standardized β = 0.162 (heteroskedasticity-robust 95% confidence interval 0.072–0.252) in DLBS and 0.097 (0.024–0.170) in AOMIC. Participant-pairs bootstrap intervals supported both associations. Replacing total tissue volume with estimated intracranial volume attenuated the AOMIC association, whereas including both preserved it. Relative macroanatomical allocation is associated with broad cognitive ability conditional on analyzed tissue volume, with differing effect magnitudes across cohorts. These cross-sectional findings do not establish causal tissue trade-offs.

item.title: Superior Frontal Gyrus Cortical Thickness Mediates the Association Between Openness to Experience and Theory of Mind: Evidence from the Human Connectome Project
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Background: Theory of mind (ToM), the capacity to infer the mental states of others, varies considerably across healthy adults. Openness to experience has been linked both to social-cognitive abilities and to thinner prefrontal cortex, but whether cortical structure statistically accounts for the association between openness and ToM is unknown. We tested whether bilateral superior frontal gyrus (SFG) cortical thickness mediates this association. Methods: Data from 1,049 healthy young adults with complete data were drawn from the Human Connectome Project. ToM was indexed by accuracy on the Heider-Simmel social animation task, openness by the NEO Five-Factor Inventory, and SFG thickness by FreeSurfer. Models adjusted for age, sex, intracranial volume and fluid intelligence; indirect effects were tested with 5,000 bootstrap resamples, and Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction was applied. Results: Openness showed a positive total effect on ToM accuracy (beta = .081, p = .009). Higher openness was associated with thinner left and right SFG (beta = -.085 and -.084), and thinner SFG with higher ToM accuracy (beta = -.082 and -.075). Indirect effects were significant (left: .0069, 95% CI [.0010, .0158]; right: .0063, 95% CI [.0007, .0146]), accounting for approximately 8.5% and 7.8% of the total effect, and remained significant after rank-based normalisation of the ceiling-affected ToM scores. Conclusions: SFG cortical thickness partially and statistically mediates the association between openness to experience and social cognition. Because the data are cross-sectional and effects are small, the findings do not establish a causal mechanism, neural efficiency or synaptic pruning, but they identify a candidate structural pathway for longitudinal testing.

item.title: Adaptive and maladaptive microstructural remodelling of the maternal brain revealed by diffusion kurtosis imaging
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Postpartum depression (PPD) is a major maternal mental health concern that may arise during neurobiological and emotional adaptation. Alterations in these adaptive processes may contribute to depressive symptom vulnerability; however, the neurobiological basis of postpartum brain adaptation remains unclear. We investigated microstructural brain remodelling in postpartum women using diffusion kurtosis imaging (DKI) and evaluated its association with Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) scores. We compared brain magnetic resonance imaging findings between 15 women one month postpartum and 10 nulliparous women without psychiatric disorders. Tract-based spatial statistics and regions of interest were analysed using diffusion tensor and kurtosis metrics. Compared with nulliparous women, postpartum women showed significantly lower mean and axial diffusivity values in white matter regions, including the frontal lobe, basal ganglia, and corticospinal tract. The posterior insular cortex showed increased mean and radial kurtosis, whereas the putamen demonstrated decreased diffusivity. EPDS scores showed positive correlations with kurtosis metrics in the amygdala and negative correlations with diffusivity metrics in the hypothalamus. These findings suggest that the postpartum brain undergoes coordinated microstructural remodelling involving emotional regulation, stress response, and maternal behavioural adaptations. Thus, DKI may provide an objective neuroimaging biomarker for identifying maladaptive postpartum brain changes associated with depressive symptoms.

item.title: Posterior cortical gray matter heterogeneity between hyposmia- and RBD-defined prodromal phenotypes in Parkinson's disease: a PPMI voxel-based morphometry study
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Background Prodromal Parkinson's disease (PD) includes clinically distinct enrollment phenotypes. We examined whole-brain gray matter volume (GMV) in Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI) participants recruited through hyposmia-only or REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD)-only pathways and assessed the stability of the findings. Methods Baseline T1-weighted MRI from 465 hyposmia-only and 149 RBD-only participants (N = 614) was analyzed with CAT12/SPM25 voxel-based morphometry (VBM). Models included age, sex, intracranial volume, and scanner family. Whole-brain clusters were defined at voxel p < 0.001 and tested using family-wise error (FWE) correction. We examined scanner-restricted samples, 123 sex/scanner-matched pairs, and 10,000-sign-flip permutation analysis of linear models (PALM). Bilateral cuneus/calcarine estimates and clinical assessments were exploratory. Results Whole-brain analysis identified a posterior phenotype effect (F cluster: k = 4,499; pFWE = 4.15×10⁻⁷), with higher GMV in hyposmia-only participants. In 123 matched pairs, a posterior H > RBD T cluster survived correction (pFWE = 0.0266), whereas the F contrast did not. PALM also identified a posterior effect (two-sided threshold-free cluster enhancement [TFCE] FWE p = 0.0027; voxelwise FWE p = 0.0277). Adjusted bilateral cuneus differences were + 0.211 mL (95% CI 0.095–0.327) in the full cohort and + 0.187 mL (0.041–0.333) after matching. MRI-proximal RBD screening questionnaire scores showed no significant association with regional GMV. Conclusions Posterior cortical GMV differed between these enrollment-defined prodromal phenotypes. The anatomical finding was supported by nonparametric inference, although the matched F test and strictest scanner restriction were nonsignificant. Longitudinal studies are needed to establish its clinical relevance.

item.title: Longitudinal Changes in the Cortico-Reticulospinal Tract Associated with High-Intensity Locomotor Training in Chronic Stroke.
item.description:
Neurorehabilitation and neural repair
Introduction High-intensity locomotor training (HIT) is recommended for improving walking capacity, but treatment responses are variable. Understanding the brain changes underlying responsiveness to training could provide insight into this variability. Emerging evidence suggests upregulation of the contralesional cortico-reticulospinal tract (CRST) may contribute to walking function after stroke. However, it is unclear whether CRST upregulation is supportive or maladaptive, and no studies have examined CRST changes after HIT. This study investigated how CRST and corticospinal tract (CST) strength and laterality reorganize, and their relationship with walking capacity after locomotor HIT. Methods Ten participants with chronic stroke completed a 4-week no-intervention control phase then 4 weeks of HIT. Diffusion MRI and 6-minute walk distance were obtained at weeks 0, 4, and 8. Analysis tested changes in ipsilesional and contralesional CRST and CST strength and laterality. Associations between changes in tract laterality and walking capacity were examined. Results During the treatment phase (vs the control phase), there were significantly greater increases in contralesional CRST strength (1.02 SD [95% CI: 0.25, 1.79]), contralesional CRST laterality (4.44 [2.15, 6.72]), and 6-minute walk distance (33 meters [17, 50]). Walking capacity improvements were associated with changes in CRST laterality (r = 0.77, P = .01), but not CST laterality (r = -0.01, P = 0.98). Discussion Following HIT, increases in contralesional CRST strength and laterality were observed. CRST laterality changes were strongly associated with walking improvements, suggesting an association between contralesional CRST changes and training-related improvements. item.title: Six-Month Music Practice Versus Psychomotor Interventions in Mild Cognitive Impairment: Behavioral and Hippocampal Outcomes.
item.description:
Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences
Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) is characterized by measurable cognitive decline with largely preserved daily functioning and increased risk of dementia. MCI patients may also exhibit sensorimotor and communication impairments, while hippocampal atrophy and altered functional connectivity are prominent neural features associated with further cognitive decline. Evidence from nonpharmacological interventions integrating cognitive challenge, coordinated movement, and emotional engagement remains limited in early-stage MCI. In this pilot intervention study, we examined whether 6 months of intensive musical instrument training versus psychomotor interventions were associated with changes in cognitive and sensorimotor performance, hippocampal gray matter volume, and functional connectivity. Outcomes were compared between randomized MCI groups, with matched healthy controls as reference for test-retest and age-related neural effects. Improvements in global cognition were modest, reaching marginal significance only in the music group, while both interventions were associated with complementary domain-specific cognitive and sensorimotor gains. Hippocampal gray matter volume remained stable across all three groups, whereas hippocampal functional connectivity declined in healthy controls but remained stable in both intervention groups, consistent with possible functional neural maintenance. These preliminary findings suggest that group-based, low-risk music and psychomotor interventions may support cognitive, sensorimotor, and neural functioning in early MCI, warranting further investigation in larger controlled trials.

item.title: Serum brain-derived tau in lacunar stroke and cerebral small vessel disease.
item.description:
European stroke journal
Introduction Brain-derived tau (BD-tau) selectively quantifies tau of central nervous system origin in blood and has demonstrated strong correlations with infarct volume and functional outcome in general ischaemic stroke, but data in lacunar stroke and cerebral small vessel disease (CSVD) are lacking. Patients and methods In a prospectively collected cohort of 101 lacunar stroke patients with an MRI-confirmed recent small subcortical infarct (RSSI) and 47 controls, we measured serum BD-tau using the HD-X SIMOA platform at baseline and 3 and 15 months after stroke. We examined associations of BD-tau with infarct size, chronic CSVD neuroimaging features (white matter hyperintensities [WMHs], lacunes, microbleeds, total SVD score), CSVD progression on follow-up MRI and functional outcome. Results Baseline serum BD-tau was higher in RSSI patients than controls (median 9.54 [7.32-12.20] vs 7.75 [6.18-9.44] pg/mL; P = .003) and correlated with infarct diameter (rs = 0.222, P = 0.039). Brain-derived tau did not correlate with time from stroke symptom onset to blood sampling (rs = 0.150, P = .179). Brain-derived tau was not associated with chronic CSVD neuroimaging features (WMHs, lacunes, microbleeds, SVD score; all P > .05) at any timepoint. Longitudinally, BD-tau returned to control levels by 3 months (P = .374) and remained stable at 15 months (P = .985). Brain-derived tau was neither associated with new vascular MRI lesions on follow-up nor functional neurological outcome. Conclusion Serum BD-tau is elevated acutely in CSVD-related RSSI, correlates with infarct size and normalises by 3 months. Brain-derived tau was not associated with chronic CSVD neuroimaging features or disease progression, suggesting sensitivity to acute neuronal injury rather than chronic or progressive CSVD.

item.title: Diagnostic and sex effects on frontostriatal brain wiring structural organization in early psychosis affective subjects compared to healthy controls.
item.description:
Molecular psychiatry
Background Brain connectivity abnormalities may underlie affective psychosis which may be influenced by sex. Using diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (dMRI) tractography, we assessed frontostriatal brain wiring connectivity patterns in 46 early psychosis affective and 56 healthy control young adult, male and female participants. Methods We collected harmonized whole brain tractography dMRI data from three sites and applied our novel fiber clustering methodology to identify 17 white matter fiber clusters connecting the frontal cortex and caudate per hemisphere in each group. By comparing cortical and caudate inter-cluster endpoint distances between groups, we assessed their patterns of frontostriatal connectivity. Results 1) In both males and females in early affective psychosis and healthy controls, bilaterally, the frontal cortex to caudate wiring pattern deviated from a topographic organization. 2) in a right hemisphere frontal pole fiber cluster, independent of sex, we found a significant interaction effect of diagnosis on the connectivity pattern between frontal cortex and caudate, (p = 0.013); 3) in a left hemisphere inferior frontal gyrus, pars triangularis, fiber cluster, we found sex influenced the significant interaction effect of diagnosis on the connectivity pattern between frontal cortex and caudate, (p = 0.0085), with the effect much greater in females (p < 0.00001) than in males (p = 0.97); and, 4) post-hoc tests showed a significant effect of diagnosis on the pattern of frontal cortex to caudate connectivity in specific subregions (ps ≤0.04). Conclusions Importantly, while the frontostriatal wiring pattern in both early affective psychosis and healthy controls deviated from a topographic organization, we found in a right hemisphere fiber cluster, independent of sex, that a significant interaction effect of diagnosis was observed on the frontal cortex to caudate connectivity pattern, whereas, in a left hemisphere fiber cluster, the effect of diagnosis on connectivity pattern was influenced by sex, showing the importance of the role of sex in brain wiring patterns in early affective psychosis.

item.title: Hippocampal Subfield Volumes and Spatial Memory Performance in Older Adults At-Risk for Type 2 Diabetes.
item.description:
Hippocampus
Older adults at risk for type 2 diabetes (T2D) are more likely to experience accelerated cognitive aging and neurodegeneration due to impaired metabolism in the hippocampus. However, the precise relationship between T2D risk factors, brain volumes (i.e., gray matter, white matter, hippocampus subfields), and hippocampus-dependent functions (i.e., spatial pattern separation, a component of spatial memory) remains unexplored. To investigate these relationships in this cross-sectional study, 60 older adults at risk for T2D (e.g., high BMI or elevated A1c levels) completed a touchscreen-based spatial pattern separation behavioral task-the Trial-Unique delayed Nonmatching-to-Location (TUNL) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). HippUnfold was utilized to segment the hippocampus from high-resolution, T1 -weighted images. We found positive correlations between A1c levels and volumes of the dentate gyrus (DG) and cornu ammonis (CA) 2, indicating that higher A1c was associated with larger volumes of hippocampal subregions. Additionally, TUNL accuracy was correlated with gray matter and distinct hippocampus subfield volumes (i.e., subiculum, CA1, and CA4), with larger volumes associated with better spatial memory performance. Understanding early structural changes in T2D risk allows us to further characterize changes in brain health associated with metabolic dysfunction.

item.title: Fixel-wise Differences in White Matter Fiber-bundle Cross-section identified in Children who Stutter
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Developmental stuttering has been repeatedly linked to decreased white matter integrity and structural connectivity differences in major white matter tracts. Prior diffusion-weighted MRI studies reporting such white matter structural differences involved voxel-averaged tensor measures (e.g., fractional anisotropy (FA)). A well-acknowledged limitation of this approach, however, has been that it cannot resolve distinct fiber populations within crossing-fiber regions. Fixel-based analysis addresses this limitation by quantifying individual fiber populations within a voxel and providing complementary measures of fiber density (FD), fiber-bundle cross-section (FC), and their combined measure (FDC).Here we applied Fixel-based analysis to diffusion MRI data from 171 children aged 3 - 13 years, including 84 children who stutter and 87 typically developing controls, to test whether white-matter differences associated with developmental stuttering were expressed as differences in FD, FC, and FDC and whether these measures show group-specific age-related patterns. We evaluated this at both the whole-brain level and within a priori white-matter tracts.FC, but not FD or FDC, showed significant Group and Group by Age effects, indicating that white-matter differences were primarily expressed in fiber-bundle macrostructure. Tract-of-interest analyses identified developmental differences in bilateral arcuate fasciculus FC that remained significant across tracts, with controls showing greater age-related increases in FC than children who stutter. Additional FC differences were observed across corticospinal and thalamocortical pathways, although these tract-wise effects were less robust to across-tract correction. These findings suggest that white-matter differences in developmental stuttering are prominently expressed in fiber-bundle macrostructure rather than fiber density and highlight divergent development of bilateral arcuate pathways. FBA provides fiber-specific information that complements conventional tensor-based diffusion measures and may improve characterization of white-matter development in childhood stuttering.

item.title: Occupational Exposure Rather Than Trauma: Lower Occipital Gray Matter Volume in Underground Coal Miners Without PTSD or Other Psychiatric Diagnoses.
item.description:
Neurotoxicology
Underground coal mining involves extreme conditions such as inadequate lighting, chronic exposure to dust and toxic gases, and intense occupational stress. Cortical changes observed in miners have been addressed almost exclusively in the literature within the framework of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), neglecting the possibility that these changes may stem directly from environmental exposure independently of psychopathology. The potential for work-specific conditions such as prolonged dark work, insufficient daylight, and exposure to toxic dust to lead to structural brain changes even without any psychopathology has been overlooked. To address this gap, 28 underground miners and 28 surface miners, who were free of current psychiatric and neurological diagnoses, were compared. T1 images obtained from 3T MRI were analyzed using voxel-based morphometry (VBM) with CAT12/SPM12. Relationships between gray matter volume, working time, and neuropsychological performance were examined using a generalized additive model (GAM). Significantly lower gray matter volume was detected in the left occipital cortex (calcarine fissure, lingual and inferior occipital gyrus) of miners (t(53) = 4.82, pFWE = 0.026, d = 1.32). The effect was regionally selective. Occipital volume was negatively correlated with underground work time (r = -0.422), while this correlation was absent in the control group (r = 0.013). GAM showed significant nonlinear relationships between morphometry and learning score, recall and TMT-B (R² = 89%). This study is one of the first to associate occipital volume reduction in miners with chronic occupational exposure independently of psychological trauma. The findings are critically important for occupational health policies targeting neurological protection.

item.title: Distinct gradients of cortical architecture capture visual representations and behavior across the lifespan.
item.description:
eLife
The microstructure of cells within the human cerebral cortex varies across the cortical ribbon, where changes in cytoarchitecture and myeloarchitecture are thought to endow each region of the cortex with its unique function. While fine-scale relative to a cell, these changes at the population level impact architectural properties of the cortex measurable in vivo by noninvasive MRI, such as the thickness and myelin content of the cortex. This raises the question of whether or not we can use these in vivo architectural measures to understand cortical organization, function, and development more broadly. Using the human visual cortex as a test bed, we demonstrated two architectural gradients, one in which cytoarchitecture and myeloarchitecture converge and another in which they diverge. These two gradients underlie the structural and functional topography of the visual cortex, even predicting the presence of new visual representations. Moreover, the two gradients show distinct visual behavior relevance and lifespan trajectory. These findings provide a more general framework for understanding the human cortex, showing that architectural gradients are a measurable fingerprint of functional organization and ontogenetic routines in the human brain.

item.title: Salience network expansion as a transdiagnostic neural marker for psychopathology risk in adolescence
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Increased cortical surface area of the brain's salience network (SAL) has been observed in depression and appears to emerge during early adolescence. However, similar expansion has also been reported in bipolar disorder (BD), obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD), and other atypicalities of salience network function have been broadly implicated across multiple psychiatric conditions. Whether increased SAL surface area is specific to depression or related more generally with psychopathology remains unclear. Using data collected as part of the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study (baseline: N = 7942; ages 9-10; Year 2: N = 5901; ages 11-12), we quantified individual SAL size and examined associations with dimensional symptoms from the Child Behavior Checklist. SAL surface area showed substantial inter-individual variability, with expansion occurring primarily through encroachment into the default mode (DMN), action-mode (AMN), and frontoparietal (FP) networks. Larger SAL size showed a modest positive association with depressive symptoms in the baseline sample, consistent with prior reports; however, this association did not replicate in the year 2 internal replication sample. Instead, associations with total problems were stronger and replicated across both timepoints, suggesting a subtle, dimensional relationship between SAL organization and general psychopathology burden. These findings suggest that individual differences in SAL organization may represent a broader transdiagnostic neural correlate of dimensional psychopathology rather than a disorder-specific neural signature.

item.title: Algorithmic Geometry Shapes the Biological Meaning of Thalamocortical Structural Covariance
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Neuroimaging studies often derive and discuss structural covariance (SC) as a representation of underlying brain circuitry that reflects coordinated maturation, anatomical connectivity, transcriptional similarity, and shared genetic influences. These associations motivate its use to study brain organization across development, aging, and disease. However, the algorithms used to derive SC networks impose constraints that may shape their biological interpretation. To understand the impact of algorithm choice, we used the thalamocortical system as an example and compared five common representations of voxelwise SC, namely, principal component analysis (PCA), independent component analysis (ICA), non-negative matrix factorization (NMF), orthogonal projective NMF (OPNMF), and \textit{k}-means clustering, in 755 participants aged 8--22 years from the Philadelphia Neurodevelopmental Cohort (PNC). SC networks derived from deformation-based morphometry (DBM) were evaluated against three complementary biological benchmarks: age-related individual differences, fractional-anisotropy (FA)-based microstructural connectivity of regionally-specific thalamocortical connections, and Allen Human Brain Atlas gene expression. Each algorithm demonstrated underlying sensitivity to differing aspects of neurobiology: PCA and OPNMF showed the strongest associations between participant-level component weights and age. NMF, OPNMF, and \textit{k}-means showed greater spatial overlap between positive cortical SC and tractography-derived projections. ICA and PCA showed stronger correspondence between thalamic and cortical gene-expression profiles across the transcriptome, whereas NMF, OPNMF, and \textit{k}-means more often identified thalamic components with relatively high core-matrix gene expression. This study emphasizes that algorithmic constraints effectively act as biological priors and decomposition methods do not provide neutral compression of the data. We conclude that it is critical to consider whether the algorithmic objective matches the representational geometry of the neurobiology being studied. Overall, our findings suggest that SC studies should select and justify algorithms according to the biological question, explicitly considering whether their constraints favour distributed gradients, overlapping regional parts, or discrete clusters. Meanwhile, interpretations of SC findings could also be informed by the specific algorithmic constraints used to derive them.

item.title: Constantin von Economo (1876-1931): cytoarchitectonic roots of modern network neuroscience.
item.description:
Journal of neurosurgery
Constantin von Economo (1876-1931) is widely remembered for his seminal description of encephalitis lethargica, yet his broader contribution to cortical organization remains underappreciated. Beyond clinical neurology, von Economo and Georg Koskinas, a neurologist-psychiatrist, contributed to the broader cytoarchitectonic tradition by developing one of the most detailed architectonic frameworks of the human cerebral cortex, emphasizing laminar heterogeneity, regional transition, and structural specialization. These concepts can be reconsidered in relation to contemporary models of large-scale brain organization. In particular, cortical territories associated with von Economo's work, including the anterior insula and anterior cingulate region, are now recognized as key hubs in salience processing and contain the distinctive spindle-shaped neurons later termed von Economo neurons. Recent advances in connectomics, cortical gradient mapping, and laminar neuroimaging have renewed interest in the relationship between cortical microstructure and distributed functional networks. From this perspective, von Economo's work may be viewed not simply as a landmark in classical neuroanatomy, but as a historically important structural framework that can be reinterpreted in relation to modern ideas of structure-function coupling and network-level brain organization. This historical vignette revisits his life, scientific contributions, and enduring relevance to contemporary neuroscience and neurosurgical thinking.

item.title: A case study of early-emerging prosopometamorphopsia.
item.description:
Cognitive neuropsychology
Prosopometamorphopsia (PMO) is a rare perceptual disorder characterized by facial distortions. This report presents the first thorough study of early-emerging PMO. Zed, who was 15 years old when first tested, has experienced lifelong, dynamic facial distortions in which features move, droop, disappear, expand, and rotate. He also experiences identity misrecognitions, perceiving familiar faces as strangers and vice versa. Behavioural assessments indicate Zed's distortions persist across different viewpoints, visual field positions, picture-plane orientations, and visual angles. Neuropsychological testing revealed deficits in face identity recognition, yet Zed performed normally on tests requiring fine-grained perception of facial age and sex. While structural MRI showed no lesions, MRI revealed reduced face-selectivity in right posterior face-selective areas, and diffusion tensor imaging indicated lower white matter integrity in the left inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus. This case offers novel insights into the manifestations of early-emerging PMO, its co-occurrence with other face-processing disorders, and its underlying neural correlates.

item.title: Association of Neighborhood Opportunity and Abdominal Obesity with Brain Development and Cognitive Function in Adolescents: A Prospective Cohort Analysis.
item.description:
Annals of epidemiology
Objective To investigate the longitudinal associations between neighborhood opportunity and brain structure and cognitive performance among adolescents, and to explore whether these associations differ by sex, maturational status, race/ethnicity, and abdominal obesity trajectory. Methods Prospective data from ABCD Study participants with complete baseline data (n = 9,375; ages 9-10 years, 47% girls; 21 U.S. sites), followed from 2016-2018 to 2020-2022, were analyzed; outcome-specific analytic samples were 9,121 at 2 years and 3,048 at 4 years. Neighborhood opportunity was measured with the Childhood Opportunity Index (COI) 2.0, subcortical volumes with MRI, and cognition with the NIH Toolbox. Mixed-effects models adjusted for baseline outcome, age, sex, race/ethnicity, population density, and time-varying waist-to-height ratio; sex differences were tested directly. Results Mean (SD) baseline age was 9.9 (0.6) years, and 54.4% were White. Very-high versus very-low COI was associated with larger subcortical volumes (e.g., amygdala 25.33 mm³; 95% CI 11.98 to 38.69, at 2 years) and higher memory scores at 2 years (5.56 points; 4.55 to 6.57) and 4 years (6.68; 4.44 to 8.91). Associations with the amygdala (2 years) and caudate (both waves) were larger in girls than in boys; cognitive associations did not differ by sex. Four-year estimates were similar to or larger than 2-year estimates; loss of statistical significance reflected the smaller 4-year samples. Conclusions Adolescents from socioeconomically disadvantaged environments experience significant disparities in brain structure and cognitive function, which exploratory stratified analyses suggesting variation by abdominal obesity and sociodemographic characteristics including sex, maturational status, and race/ethnicity.

item.title: The impact of pruning iterations on Arcuate Fasciculus morphometry and diffusion features in right-handed adults.
item.description:
Radiological physics and technology
To evaluate the utility of a pruning method in refining tractography and to examine the Arcuate Fasciculus (AF) morphometry and diffusion metrics in right-handed adults. Thirty-two healthy, right-handed adults underwent DTI on a 1.5T MRI system. Q-space diffeomorphic reconstruction was performed on a single-shell DTI dataset, and the AF was automatically tracked. Topology-Informed Pruning (TIP) was applied to reduce false-positive streamlines across varying numbers of iterations. Morphometry and diffusion metrics of the bilateral AF were extracted. The associations between these metrics and the number of iterations were evaluated using correlation analysis. The protocol-specific TIP threshold was identified as the knee point using the Kneedle algorithm. Differences in the morphometry and diffusion metrics of the selection AF tractometry by sex and hemisphere were also examined. A pFDR < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. TIP-based pruning was associated with improved tract delineation through the reduction of spurious streamlines. The number of pruning iterations affected the AF's morphometry and diffusion metrics. The selected TIP threshold was 8, and TIPs greater than 8 yielded stable values with minimal variability. Significant differences between hemispheres were observed in diffusion metrics except quantitative anisotropy (QA). For morphometry metrics, significant differences were identified in the number of tracts, span, and curl (pFDR < 0.05). No significant sex-related differences were found after FDR correction. Pruning iterations affect the visualization of AF in the protocol-specific population of right-handed adults. The number of pruning iterations selected should be carefully determined with full awareness and consideration.

item.title: Brain and Cardiometabolic Effects of Major Weight Loss in People With Obesity: Preliminary Cohort Findings.
item.description:
Obesity science & practice
Objective Given the overlap between obesity-related metabolic and vascular abnormalities and Alzheimer's disease (AD) risk factors, it is critical to determine whether weight loss improves brain and cardiovascular health. This study examined whether ≥ 40% excess-weight loss is associated with improvements in cardiometabolic risk, brain structure, and cognition. Methods The study was a longitudinal study of individuals with obesity undergoing metabolic and bariatric surgery or medical/behavioral weight-loss treatment. Participants were classified at follow-up as weight-loss (WL; ≥ 40% excess-weight loss) or non-weight-loss (nWL; < 40%). All completed medical evaluations, structural MRI, and cognitive testing at baseline and 1 year. Results At 1 year, the WL group exhibited improvements in BMI, HbA1C, inflammatory, metabolic, and lipid profiles. MRI-based volumetrics revealed increases in subcortical gray-matter volume and preservation of AD-vulnerable regions. Cognitive performance remained unchanged. Conclusions Achieving ≥ 40% excess-weight loss was associated with improvements in metabolic health and brain structure, including favorable subcortical volume increases. These findings underscore the potential of sustained weight reduction to mitigate risks linked to metabolic syndromes and neurodegeneration. Longer-term follow-up is warranted to determine whether continued metabolic improvements lead to detectable cognitive gains and additional brain-health benefits beyond 1 year.

item.title: In Utero MRI of Radial Glial Fibers Highlights Their Role in Modulating Fetal Cortical Folding
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
The process of cortical folding is fundamental to early human brain development. While the differential growth of the cortical layers is a known driver, the biomechanical contribution of key cellular microstructures remains unclear, and there is a lack of direct in vivo markers of cortical microstructures for time-resolved observations. Using a multimodal approach combining in utero and ex vivo fetal brain MRI, histology, and computational mechanical simulation, we investigated whether developmental reorganization of cortical radial microstructures, particularly the radial glial cell (RGC)-associated scaffold, is linked to cortical folding and may modulate its mechanical progression. We characterized this radial organization noninvasively using diffusion MRI-based radial fiber density ( FD rad ). ex vivo fetal brain MRI and histology supported that regional variations in FD rad were strongly associated with vimentin-labelled radial architecture. Our in utero MRI data revealed closely coordinated developmental changes in cortical FD rad and curvature, with their regional timings and spatial patterns significantly coupled across the cortex. Longitudinal in utero MRI data further supported the synchronized within-individual co-development of FD rad and curvature. Furthermore, biomechanical simulations showed that reducing radial reinforcement modulated differential-growth-driven buckling, producing earlier folding and a greater cortical curvature under otherwise matched model conditions. Collectively, this study introduces FD rad as a noninvasive in utero MRI measure sensitive to radial glial fibers. By integrating spatial, temporal, histological, and computational evidence, our findings suggested a model in which developmental disassembly of the radial scaffold may modulate the mechanical response of the fetal cortex to differential growth, thereby contributing to cortical folding.

item.title: The Aging Brain Matrix: Cross-Species Evidence Linking FREM3 to Brain and Cognitive Aging
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract The human extracellular-matrix-related FREM3 gene is strongly age-dependent, enriched in age-sensitive excitatory long-range-projecting neurons, and implicated in neurodegenerative diseases. To establish the first translationally relevant causal evidence for the gene’s roles in brain structure and cognition, we developed an excitatory-neuron-specific Frem3 conditional knockout mouse model ( Frem3 -cKO) and computed genetically regulated expression of FREM3 ( FREM3 -GReX) in humans, enabling convergent neurostructural and cognitive characterizations. Frem3 -cKO mice showed widespread lower global and regional brain volume in middle age vs young adulthood, consistent with drastic age-dependent volume loss absent in wildtype mice. These effects were strongest in cognitively relevant cortical regions and paralleled by lower cognitive performance. In humans, lower FREM3- GReX was associated with lower total surface area, which further mediated an indirect link to lower cognitive performance across multiple age-sensitive domains. We provide the first translationally relevant cross-species evidence supporting a key role for FREM3/Frem3 in maintaining brain and cognitive health across aging.

item.title: A Wasserstein Weisfeiler-Lehman Kernel Framework for Multimodal Brain Connectome Analysis
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract We introduce a Wasserstein Weisfeiler-Lehman (WWL) graph-kernel framework for the joint analysis of weighted structural graphs and continuous node attributes, together with a regularized fractional-Laplacian extension of the underlying graph propagation operator. The proposed fractional operator provides non-local propagation across the entire graph, with influence decaying as a power law with graph distance, while remaining anchored to the subject-specific structural topology. This extends the standard finite-range Weisfeiler Lehman propagation scheme to a controlled long-range setting without introducing an externally prescribed coupling between structural and functional information. We formulate the framework for multimodal brain connectivity by representing each subject as a single attributed graph: diffusion tractography defines the weighted structural edges, while resting-state functional connectivity profiles are encoded as continuous node attributes. We evaluate the method on a synthetic cohort of $900$ subjects in three ordered clinical groups along the Alzheimer's disease spectrum, generated from multiple structural templates and characterised by a spatially structured loss of resting-state network segregation with age. Under nested cross-validation, the WWL kernel achieves a balanced accuracy of $0.651\pm0.028$, significantly outperforming both a raw-feature SVM and a histogram-based WL-kernel baseline. Controlled ablations separate the contribution of the Wasserstein representation from that of structural propagation. Replacing the propagation operator by the identity yields essentially identical classification performance, whereas a structure-only representation approaches chance, showing that the discriminative gain in this benchmark is primarily associated with the Wasserstein point-cloud representation rather than structural propagation. Conversely, experiments across distinct signal regimes show that the fractional extension is signal-dependent: non-local propagation can improve continuous prediction for diffuse whole-brain coupling signals, but provides no consistent advantage for network-segregation signals. We further identify a connectivity artefact induced by fixed-percentile structural sparsification and establish a threshold preserving graph connectivity across subjects. The results clarify the respective roles of Wasserstein geometry, structural propagation, and non-locality in multimodal graph representations and provide a controlled framework for assessing when fractional graph propagation is expected to be beneficial.

item.title: From Brain Structure to Stress Response: COVID-Specific Anxiety Links Pre-Pandemic Gray Matter Volume to Changes in Life Satisfaction.
item.description:
Depression and anxiety
The COVID-19 pandemic severely threatened mental well-being, potentially impacting individual life satisfaction (LS); thus, this study sought to identify pre-pandemic brain structural markers associated with subsequent LS changes and explore the role of COVID-specific anxiety in this relationship. We utilized structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and behavioral data (including the LS scale) collected before the pandemic (T1) from 115 general university students, followed up 1 year after the outbreak (T2) for LS and COVID-anxiety measures. Employing whole-brain voxel-based morphometry (VBM) and confirmatory prediction analyses, we identified brain regions where pre-pandemic gray matter volume (GMV) correlated with subsequent LS changes (ΔLS from T1 to T2), followed by mediation analysis to assess the indirect effect of COVID-anxiety. While group-level ΔLS was stable, individual variability showed a significant negative correlation with pre-pandemic GMV in the pregenual anterior cingulate cortex (pgACC) and left superior temporal gyrus (STG), and a positive correlation with GMV in right precuneus. Furthermore, COVID-anxiety correlated with ΔLS, and mediation analysis revealed a significant negative indirect effect of COVID-anxiety on the link between pgACC GMV and ΔLS, such that greater pre-pandemic pgACC GMV was associated with higher COVID-specific anxiety, which in turn was associated with a decrease in LS. This mediation effect was partial, as the direct path from pgACC GMV to ΔLS remained significant. Crucially, these results were independent of socioeconomic status, stressful life events, and general mental health. Overall, our study indicates that pre-pandemic brain structure can prospectively predict individual LS changes during the pandemic, and this relationship was mediated by COVID-specific anxiety. These findings shed light on the neuroanatomical basis of LS and could have implications for targeted interventions during public health crises and similar challenges.

item.title: Cerebellar subregions support social cognition in early behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia.
item.description:
Brain : a journal of neurology
Social cognitive deficits manifest early in behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD), compromising individuals' ability to interpret social cues, empathize, and maintain interpersonal relationships. Current neurobiological models emphasize cortical network disruption, particularly within the salience, semantic appraisal, and default mode networks, as primary contributors to social dysfunction. However, despite the increasingly recognized role of the cerebellum in higher-order cognitive and socioemotional processes, its contributions to social deficits remains underexplored in bvFTD. Here, we investigated the unique and network-level influences of cerebellar subregions on social cognition across experimental and real-world assessments in early-stage bvFTD. A total of 107 individuals with bvFTD and 100 healthy controls were evaluated across three social domains: theory of mind (ToM) (The Awareness of Social Inference Test-Social Inference-Enriched, TASIT-SIE; Cognitive Emotional Perspective Taking Test), emotion reading (Dynamic Affect Recognition Test; TASIT-Emotion Evaluation Test; Comprehensive Affect Testing System), and real-life empathy (Revised Self-Monitoring Scale; Interpersonal Reactivity Index). Using a functional cerebellar parcellation, we extracted volumes of posterior cerebellar subregions implicated in social-linguistic and multiple-demand networks from participants' structural MRIs. To address the high collinearity between cerebellar and cortical atrophy patterns, we applied sequential regression, partial least squares correlation, and dominance analysis to characterize brain-behavior relationships. Additionally, supplementary structural equation modelling (SEM) examined whether the associations between cerebellar integrity and social cognition was mediated by executive functioning. Our results showed that cerebellar subregional integrity contributed to social cognitive deficits in individuals with early-stage bvFTD. Cerebellar subregions, particularly right Crus I and II, showed the strongest and most selective contribution to high-level inferential Theory of Mind performance. Tasks involving dynamic emotion stimuli exhibited a more distributed pattern of cerebello-cerebral involvement. By contrast, questionnaire-based measures of real-world social functioning were less prominently represented in the latent covariance structure. SEM further showed that cerebellar integrity remained directly associated with social cognition after accounting for executive functioning, whereas the indirect association through executive functioning was not significant. These findings highlight the task-dependent nature of cerebellar involvement in social cognition, and demonstrate that time-limited experimental tasks, particularly those involving inferential reasoning about beliefs and affect, are likely to be especially valuable in detecting subtle cerebello-cerebral network dysfunction that questionnaire-based measures may overlook. Our results extend cortex-centric models of social dysfunction in bvFTD by demonstrating that cerebellar subregions contribute to distributed cerebello-cerebral systems associated with social cognitive performance. These findings provide a foundation for future longitudinal and mechanistic studies of cerebello-cerebral dysfunction in neurodegenerative disease.

item.title: Cross-metric convergence reveals altered white matter microstructural-functional correspondence in bipolar ii disorder.
item.description:
Journal of affective disorders
Background White matter (WM) microstructural abnormalities are increasingly recognized in bipolar II disorder (BD-II), but it remains unclear how tract-wise microstructural organization corresponds to WM functional connectivity. Methods Diffusion MRI and resting-state fMRI data were acquired from 86 patients with BD-II and 84 healthy controls (HCs). Microstructural profile similarity (MPS) and functional connectivity (FC) matrices were constructed across 48 WM tracts. Following participant-wise, modality-specific standardization of the MPS and FC matrices, tract-wise correspondence was quantified using Spearman correlation and Euclidean profile distance, with self-connections excluded. Group differences were assessed using covariate-adjusted linear models with false discovery rate correction. Sensitivity analyses assessed robustness to clinical sample restrictions and methodological choices. Results BD-II showed altered MPS-FC correspondence in a restricted set of WM tracts, with 4 tracts identified by Spearman correlation and 6 by Euclidean distance. The left posterior corona radiata (PCR_L) and left external capsule (EC_L) showed convergent abnormalities across both metrics, characterized by higher rank-order correspondence and lower profile distance in BD-II. These convergent findings were stable across several sensitivity analyses but were sensitive to the diffusion-feature normalization reference and Euclidean profile scaling. Neither tract was significantly associated with symptom severity after multiple-comparison correction, whereas exploratory analyses implicated the left uncinate fasciculus in depressive symptom variation. Conclusions BD-II is associated with altered correspondence between WM microstructural and functional organization. These findings provide multimodal evidence for atypical WM organization and extend current understanding of the neurobiological alterations associated with BD-II.

item.title: Gray matter alterations and their atlas-based spatial associations with neurotransmitter distributions in isolated REM sleep behavior disorder.
item.description:
Sleep & breathing = Schlaf & Atmung
Purpose Multiple neurotransmitter systems are implicated in the pathophysiology of isolated rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder (iRBD) and its progression to α-synucleinopathy. This study aimed to identify baseline gray matter (GM) alterations in patients with iRBD compared with healthy controls and to examine their spatial correspondence with known neurotransmitter distributions. We further characterized GM patterns associated with future phenoconversion and their neurochemical context. Methods A total of 109 patients with iRBD who completed at least one follow-up evaluation and 24 age- and sex-matched healthy controls underwent structural magnetic resonance imaging. Gray matter volume (GMV) alterations were assessed using the CAT12 toolbox. Spatial correlations between group-level GMV difference maps and neurotransmitter atlases were evaluated using the JuSpace toolbox. Results At baseline, patients with iRBD showed reduced GMV in the right cerebellar cortex and vermis, along with increased GMV in the left putamen and pallidum. These GMV alterations demonstrated significant spatial correspondence with dopaminergic receptor and transporter maps, including dopamine D2 receptors and the dopamine transporter (DAT). Among patients with iRBD, those who subsequently phenoconverted exhibited lower baseline GMV in the right medial orbital gyrus compared with non-converters. This pattern showed significant spatial correlations with serotonergic (5-HT2A), glutamatergic (mGluR5), GABAergic (GABAa), and dopaminergic (FDOPA) neurotransmitter maps. Conclusion Patients with iRBD exhibit distinct patterns of GMV alteration that spatially align with dopaminergic neurotransmitter distribution maps, while phenoconversion is associated with GM changes corresponding to multiple neurotransmitter systems, although the phenoconversion findings are exploratory.

item.title: Prefrontal circuitry abnormalities and cognitive impairment in adolescents with early-onset psychosis.
item.description:
European child & adolescent psychiatry
Early-onset psychosis (EOP) is associated with marked cognitive impairment and poorer health-related and psychosocial outcomes compared to adult-onset illness, yet the neural mechanisms underlying these deficits during adolescence remain incompletely understood. Despite evidence implicating dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) dysfunction, the region's functional and structural correlates in youth with EOP are not well characterized. Adolescents with EOP (N=31) and healthy controls (HC; N=20) completed NIH Toolbox cognitive assessments and PROMIS self-reports. Prefrontal function was assessed using functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) during a Stroop task and at rest. Multimodal MRI, including resting-state fMRI, diffusion tensor imaging, and structural imaging, was used to examine connectivity and morphology of prefrontal and fronto-cerebellar circuits. Adolescents with EOP exhibited poorer cognitive performance across executive functioning domains compared to HC. fNIRS revealed reduced right dlPFC activation on a cognitive control paradigm (p=0.007, pfdr=0.04) and a trend of increased resting-state connectivity between right dlPFC and ventrolateral PFC (p=0.02, pfdr=0.9). Furthermore, resting-state fMRI showed increased dlPFC-striatal connectivity with striatal regions and reduced connectivity with cerebellar Crus I/II (p-FDR<0.05). White matter integrity of the superior longitudinal fasciculus correlated with dlPFC activation during task performance. Structural analyses identified reduced frontal cortical thickness and decreased cerebellar Crus II volumes (p-FWE<0.05) in patients with EOP, with frontal morphology associating with cognitive measures. Cognitive impairment in adolescents with EOP is associated with convergent abnormalities in dlPFC function, fronto-striatal connectivity, and fronto-cerebellar structure. These findings provide preliminary support for a model of disrupted prefrontal circuitry in EOP and highlight the potential clinical value of multimodal imaging markers.

item.title: Claustrum Morphometry Reveals Spatially Heterogeneous Alterations in 22q11DS
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Abstract. The human claustrum is a small, irregular, and complexly positioned structure, yet it carries long range projections to most cortical regions responsible for executive functioning. Prior structural MRI research has largely relied on global volume as the metric of its morphology. Such measures may obscure regionally specific morphological changes relevant to developmental and pathological variation. We therefore addressed this limitation by applying longitudinal surface-based morphometry to 874 scans from 440 individuals aged 5–35 years, comparing typical development with 22q11.2 deletion syndrome (22q11DS), a genetic condition characterized by brain dysmaturation, and assessing associations with working memory performance. Our data show a significant age-related volumetric decline that is reduced in 22q11DS left claustra, while surface deformation and thickness analyses revealed spatial patterns unique to hemisphere, group, and developmental age. In controls, the claustrum surface deformed with age in clustered zones along a dorsoventral gradient, and the dorsal-anterior zone thinned across development while the ventral zone thickened. 22q11DS claustra showed less age-related deformation than controls, whose claustrum surface changes associated with verbal working memory. This structural correlate was statistically equivalent to zero in carriers, consistent with a disrupted claustral development to the working memory vulnerability of the syndrome. These findings show the value of surface-based morphometry over volume alone, highlight dysmaturation and regionally organized claustrum shape variation, and suggest that disrupted structural organization is accompanied by a weaker claustrum-working memory association.

item.title: Impact of Chatbot-Based Cognitive Training on Cognitive Function and White Matter Integrity in Cognitively Unimpaired Older Adults: Randomized Controlled Trial.
item.description:
JMIR aging
Background Cognitive training may enhance cognition and support brain health during aging, but few trials have evaluated readily accessible chatbot-based programs with neuroimaging outcomes. Objective This study aimed to evaluate the effects of a chatbot-based cognitive training program on white matter microstructural organization and cognition in cognitively unimpaired older adults. Methods In a single-blind randomized controlled trial, 72 cognitively unimpaired older adults were assigned to chatbot-based cognitive training (30 min/day, 5 days/week for 12 weeks; n=37) or a no-intervention control (n=35). Diffusion tensor imaging at baseline and 12 weeks quantified fractional anisotropy (FA) in predefined white matter tracts, and cognition was assessed with the Cambridge Neuropsychological Test Automated Battery. Results Groups were comparable at baseline. After 12 weeks, the training group showed significantly less FA reduction than controls in the bilateral tapetum and right posterior thalamic radiation, surviving false discovery rate control (P<.05). The training group also improved on Paired Associates Learning (PAL), an episodic memory measure (P=.04). PAL improvement was positively associated with FA change in the right posterior thalamic radiation and right sagittal stratum (false discovery rate-adjusted P=.04 for each). Conclusions These findings suggest that a 12-week chatbot-based cognitive training program may support episodic memory and the relative maintenance of white matter microstructural organization in selected pathways in cognitively unimpaired older adults, consistent with a brain-maintenance framework. Trial registration CRIS KCT0004630; https://tinyurl.com/4xfesb68.

item.title: Individualized structural brain network and transcriptomic characterization of heterogeneity in type 2 diabetes mellitus.
item.description:
Neuroscience
Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is a heterogeneous metabolic disorder that also affects the brain, yet prior neuroimaging studies have predominantly focused on group-level comparisons, obscuring interindividual variability in brain structural organization. To capture this heterogeneity, we constructed individualized differential structural covariance networks for 156 individuals with T2DM using 148 healthy controls as a normative reference. Unsupervised clustering based on these individualized networks revealed two neuroanatomical subtypes with distinct network configurations. Most subtype-differentiating edges showed higher values in one subtype, whereas a smaller set of edges, primarily involving the basal ganglia and cerebellum, showed higher values in the other. Integration with transcriptomic data from the Allen Human Brain Atlas identified genes spatially associated with subtype-related differences. These genes were enriched in processes including receptor tyrosine kinase signaling and glycerolipid metabolism, with preferential expression in the striatum and cerebellum. Together, these findings characterize interindividual variation in brain structural covariance in T2DM and identify candidate molecular processes associated with the observed subtype differences.

item.title: Graph Neural Network Reveals the Cortical Morphology of Local Brain Aging in Normal Cognition and Alzheimer's Disease.
item.description:
Neuroinformatics
Estimating brain age (BA) from T1 -weighted magnetic resonance images (MRIs) provides a powerful framework for quantifying anatomical brain aging. Whereas global BA (GBA) summarizes overall brain health, local BA (LBA) provides cortically specific patterns of aging at the subject level. Although previous studies have examined anatomical contributors to GBA, to our knowledge, no framework has been established to estimate LBA using cortical morphology. To address this gap, we introduce a graph neural network (GNN) that uses morphometric features-cortical thickness, surface area, curvature, gray/white matter intensity ratio (GWR), sulcal depth-to estimate LBA across the cortical surface at high spatial resolution (mean inter-vertex distance = 1.37 mm). Trained on cortical surface meshes extracted from the MRIs of cognitively normal (CN) adults (N = 14,423), our model achieves better test-retest performance than the existing state-of-the-art, while identifying more biologically plausible patterns of aging in Alzheimer's disease (AD) on the ADNI dataset. Association cortices emerge as primary sites of morphometric aging in CNs, whereas mild cognitive impairment is characterized by widespread aging that is pronounced in the parahippocampal gyrus. AD subjects demonstrate significant aging across the entire cortex, particularly within medial temporal regions and associated cortical networks. Feature ablation highlights curvature and GWR as preferentially sensitive to AD pathology. Regional LBA gaps are significantly associated with neuropsychological measures of AD-related cognitive impairment, linking cortical aging patterns to clinical outcomes. These results demonstrate that GNN-based modeling of cortical morphometry enables biologically interpretable mapping of local brain aging with greater fidelity than prior work.

item.title: Microstructure of white matter association tracts in the temporal lobe predicts the timing of electrophysiological activity and behaviour in picture naming
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
White matter (WM) microstructure has been mainly associated with accuracy of picture naming. However, little is known about how WM properties relate to the timing of picture naming and its underlying electrophysiological activity. Here, we linked diffusion-weighted, electrophysiological, and behavioural data, using time-based measures to conceptually connect WM deterioration to alterations in conduction speed and precision. Our sample included individuals of varying age, with or without stroke. We correlated fractional anisotropy (FA) of bilateral WM tracts traversing the temporal lobe with mean response times (RTs) and response time variability (coefficient of variation, CV) in picture naming, and with the onset latency of neuronal activity, represented by the electrophysiological P2 component time-locked to picture onset. We selected tracts showing associations with P2 latency and naming performance separately, on which we conducted path analyses examining the relationship between structure, neuronal activity and behaviour. Depending on the tract, higher FA was associated with faster and/or more consistent naming, suggesting that ventral tracts differentially contribute to naming speed and consistency. Importantly, path modelling for the right inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus (IFOF) revealed that FA predicted P2 latency, which in turn predicted RTs, possibly reflecting a structure-activity-behaviour relationship in lexical-semantic processing. P2 source reconstruction demonstrated anatomical proximity to posterior segments of the right IFOF, supporting these findings. Overall, this study provides a proof of concept for modelling structure-activity-behaviour relationships in language research, while highlighting the need for elaboration of such relations at a more mechanistic level.

item.title: Habitual sleep duration is associated with the cortical organisation of brain network controllability
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Sleep is fundamental to adaptive brain function, yet how habitual sleep relates to the structural network properties that support flexible transitions between brain states remains poorly understood. Combining wrist-accelerometer sleep measures with diffusion MRI connectomes from 15,799 UK Biobank adults, we show that longer workday sleep is associated with higher modal controllability of somatomotor systems and lower controllability of visual cortex. This system-specific signature reproduced in a locked test set (n = 4,740) and was robust across extensive sensitivity analyses. Decomposition showed that it reflects a redistribution of structural connection weight, with greater absolute visual connectivity and a smaller somatomotor share of the whole-brain total. Weekend catch-up sleep showed no comparable association. The signature was distinct from brain-ageing patterns and, across 1,226 phenotypes, related mainly to physical activity and body composition rather than cognition. These findings link everyday sleep habits to the system-specific organisation of brain network controllability.

item.title: Insula functional connectivity development follows a canonical antero-posterior axis of organization
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
The insula is a heterogeneous region associated with a range of functional domains including sensory, cognitive, and emotional processing. Cytoarchitectural and functional studies have described an antero-posterior axis of insula organization. However, the insula's functional development remains sparsely described. We delineated the development of insula resting-state functional connectivity across 562 individuals (6-22 years) using generalized additive models and population value decomposition. We show insulo-cortical functional connectivity development differs across the insula: anterior subregions have predominantly decreasing connectivity across the age range examined, whereas posterior subregions have variable connectivity that aligns with the sensorimotor-association axis. Vertex-level analysis revealed that age-related trajectories followed an antero-posterior axis that aligned with estimates of insula microstructure. Our results emphasize that the development of insula connectivity is spatially heterogeneous and aligns with known cytoarchitecture. The normative insula development described here provides a foundation for investigating how emerging psychopathology may be linked to variation in insula development.

item.title: Tetrahydrobiopterin restores oligodendrocyte maturation after hypoxic white matter injury by reprogramming translational output
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
ABSTRACT Background Complex congenital heart defects (CHDs) are frequently associated with chronic cerebral hypoxemia, leading to impaired white matter maturation. One proposed mechanism involves hypoxia-induced disruption of the nitric oxide synthase cofactor tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4), resulting in oxidative stress and impaired oligodendrocyte (OL) development. While our previous studies found BH4 supplementation improves hypoxia-induced white matter dysmaturation, the molecular mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Because OL maturation requires coordinated translational control, we hypothesized that BH4 promotes white matter maturation by restoring translation programs disrupted by hypoxia. Methods Translating Ribosome Affinity Purification sequencing (TRAP-seq) was performed on OL lineage cells isolated from transgenic ribosomal reporter mice exposed to chronic hypoxia (10.5% O₂, postnatal day 3–11) with or without daily BH4 treatment. Differential translation, weighted gene co-expression network analysis, pathway enrichment, RNAscope, and immunohistochemistry identified translational programs associated with hypoxia and BH4-mediated rescue. Results Developmental hypoxia extensively altered the OL translatome, suppressing transcripts associated with OL maturation while enriching pathways related to translational regulation and cellular stress. Network analyses identified BH4-responsive gene modules enriched for OL maturation, protein metabolism, and translation-related processes. BH4 partially reversed hypoxia-induced translational changes, restored OL maturation gene expression, and normalized nuclear localization of the lineage regulator OLIG1, consistent with recovery of maturation-associated regulatory programs. Conclusions Developmental hypoxia disrupts OL maturation through coordinated alterations in ribosome-associated gene expression and post-transcriptional regulatory pathways. BH4 promotes recovery of OL maturation programs, including restoration of translation-related networks and OLIG1 nuclear localization, providing mechanistic insight into BH4-supported white matter maturation under chronic hypoxic conditions. Research Perspective What New Question Does This Study Raise? Developmental hypoxemia in congenital heart disease remodels the oligodendrocyte translatome, raising the question of whether translational dysregulation represents a fundamental and therapeutically targetable mechanism underlying white matter dysmaturation in other forms of perinatal brain injury. What Question Should Be Addressed Next? Future studies should determine how BH4 restores ribosome-associated translation of oligodendrocyte maturation programs, establish whether these molecular changes increase myelin protein synthesis and improve long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes, and define the cross-species efficacy for clinical translation. Clinical Research Implication These findings provide a mechanistic rationale for evaluating BH4 as a neuroprotective adjunct therapy to preserve white matter development in fetuses and infants with congenital heart disease experiencing chronic cerebral hypoxemia.

item.title: Neuroimaging Correlates of Adolescent Substance Use: A Systematic Review of the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Background: Neuroimaging may help characterize brain and contextual factors associated with substance use during development. The ABCD study supports investigation of developmental pathways relevant to substance use [1]. Objective: To synthesize original ABCD publications examining MRI measures in relation to substance use and substance-related exposures. Methods: The authors screened all 2,700 publications in the ABCD corpus. Original empirical articles reporting an MRI measure of any modality and a substance use variable were eligible; methodological, conceptual, review, and commentary articles were excluded. Imaging modality, brain measures, substances, design, and association direction were extracted for descriptive synthesis. Results: The evidence considered spans morphology, white matter microstructure, resting-state connectivity, and task activation. Findings concerning youth initiation, prenatal exposure, and familial liability address distinct developmental questions. Family history and stressful life events feature in the white matter literature [2]. Findings vary by modality, exposure definition, and temporal direction, and include null associations. Conclusions: The literature suggests distributed and context-dependent neuroimaging associations. Observational designs, overlapping participants, confounding, and analytic heterogeneity limit causal interpretation and assessment of independent replication. The findings support further longitudinal investigation but do not establish a validated MRI screening tool.

item.title: Investigating the Association of Physical Activity and Muscular Fitness with Structural Brain Changes and Cognitive Performance
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Background Physical activity (PA) is a modifiable factor linked to cognitive decline, but its relationship with structural brain changes remains inconsistent. We studied associations of self-reported PA and handgrip strength with brain structure and cognition. Methods We examined middle-aged to elderly participants from the population-based Hamburg City Health Study, who underwent brain MRI and cognitive testing. PA was assessed via questionnaires (overall PA, sport participation, strength training frequency), and handgrip strength indexed muscular fitness. MRI markers included among others peak width of skeletonized mean diffusivity (PSMD), cortical thickness, and structural connectivity metrics. Cognition was assessed with CERAD-Plus subtests. Associations were examined using multivariable linear regression and mediation analysis. Results Among 2,618 participants (mean age 64 ± 8.3 years; 44% female), higher handgrip strength was associated with lower PSMD (β=-0.117, 95% CI [-0.194, -0.041]), greater cortical thickness (β = 0.100, 95% CI [0.019, 0.181]), and faster processing speed (β=-0.155, 95% CI [-0.234, -0.076]). Self-reported PA showed no associations with brain structure. Sport participation was associated with faster processing speed (β=-0.059, 95% CI [-0.105, -0.014]), better executive function (β=-0.045, 95% CI [-0.088, -0.002]), and better verbal memory (β = 0.052, 95% CI [0.007, 0.097]). PSMD partially mediated the association between handgrip strength and processing speed (ab=-0.008, 95% CI [-0.019, -0.001]). Conclusions Handgrip strength, unlike self-reported PA, was associated with brain structure and cognitive performance, highlighting the importance of PA assessment modality in brain health research. Mediation of associations between handgrip strength and cognition by PSMD suggest white matter microstructural injury as one pathway linking neuromuscular and cognitive function. Clinical Trial Registration: ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT03934957.

item.title: Metformin Preserves Regional Brain Glucose Uptake, Structure, and Functional Connectivity in Adults with Insulin Resistance.
item.description:
The Journal of clinical investigation
Background Dementia is a rapidly expanding public health problem with major socio-economic burden. Insulin resistance (IR) is a prevalent but modifiable risk factor for dementia, yet its effects on brain structure, functional connectivity, and metabolism remain incompletely understood. Methods Regional brain glucose uptake (PET), volumes (MRI), functional connectivity (fMRI), and cognition (NIH Toolbox) was measured in 72 adults with or without markers of IR. To evaluate reversibility of IR-associated brain deficits, forty older adults with IR were randomized to forty weeks of metformin or placebo, and brain measures were repeated. As a proof-of-concept experiment, we developed a conditional brain-specific insulin receptor knockout mouse and assessed brain mitochondrial function and cognition. Results In older adults with markers of IR is associated with diminished total and regional brain volumes in areas critical for neuronal connectivity, memory, and learning, including cerebral white matter and the hippocampus. Reduced functional connectivity between brain regions detrimental for cognition was also noted. Further, we demonstrated that ATP production, essential for neuronal connectivity, was diminished in neuron-specific insulin receptor knockout mice accompanied by deficits in hippocampal- and prefrontal-dependent tasks. Forty weeks of metformin improved systemic insulin sensitivity concurrent to preserved brain glucose uptake, volume, and functional connectivity within specific regions central to decision-making and learning. Metformin was also associated with an improved composite measure of processing speed and working memory. Conclusion These findings highlight IR as a key regulator of brain metabolism and support the concept that insulin sensitization can prevent neurobiological deficits in older people with IR.

item.title: Substantial evidence against sex differences in bed nucleus of the stria terminalis volume in the human brain.
item.description:
Imaging neuroscience (Cambridge, Mass.)
"The bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (BNST) is a sexually dimorphic basal forebrain region" is a claim prevalent across rodent and human neuroscience research, arising from the observation that it is substantially larger in male versus female brains. Despite the pervasiveness of this claim, which may have implications for understanding sex differences in anxiety and substance use disorders, inspection of the literature reveals a complex and nuanced picture. Research on volumetric human BNST sex differences comes from a handful of mostly small-scale post-mortem studies and two MRI studies, between them reporting no, moderate, or very large differences. This indicates the need for a more detailed systematic investigation. Addressing this, we developed a novel 3T T1-weighted (T1w) manual segmentation protocol for the BNST, which was applied to sub-millimetre resolution T1w structural MRI data in 170 young human adults. Using a Bayesian modelling approach, taking into account existing data and accounting for total brain volume, age, and sibship, we find substantial evidence favouring no sex difference in total BNST volume. We recommend that researchers exercise caution when reporting evidence of BNST sexual dimorphism, particularly when translating findings from rodent models in which the BNST may play a different, olfaction-focused, role.

item.title: Longitudinal quantitative streamline tractography: Robust estimation of white matter connectivity differences.
item.description:
Imaging neuroscience (Cambridge, Mass.)
Longitudinal probing of structural connectivity via diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (dMRI) is experiencing uptake. However, the detection of biological effects is significantly hampered by the limitations of cross-sectional streamline tractography, where even small changes in the dMRI signal can produce drastically different trajectories and, therefore, quantitative parameterisation; if not properly dealt with, such effects will manifest as spurious longitudinal change, which can obscure subtle biological differences. To address this challenge, we here introduce a novel quantitative streamline tractography framework tailored for longitudinal analysis, wherein an individual's streamline trajectories remain fixed throughout the analysis, allowing only their ascribed density weights to vary between sessions. We present two strategies by which these quantitative streamline weights can be determined, both extensions of the widely adopted SIFT2 method. The performance of this framework is benchmarked against cross-sectional reconstruction with and without SIFT2 optimisation, in both in silico dMRI phantoms with known ground truths and three distinct human in vivo cohorts with clear a priori expectations of biological effects. We demonstrate that the proposed framework drastically reduces methodological imprecisions in synthetic dMRI phantoms and enhances statistical sensitivity and specificity to biological effects in human cohorts, enabling more robust quantification of longitudinal structural connectivity differences.
